implementation_notes: Sequences offer the same functions as Iterable but execute the whole chain lazily, one element at a time, so no intermediate collection is built and stages are the named operators (filter, map, transform) on the chain (kotlinlang.org sequences). The terminal operation (toList, sum, first) is what runs the pipeline, replacing the classic stage list and driver. Use the Flow variant when any stage suspends or the values arrive over time.
code_sketch:
val pipeline: Sequence<Row> = rows.asSequence()
    .filter { it.isNotBlank() }
    .map(::parse)
    .map(::enrich)

pipeline.take(10).toList()   // terminal operation runs the chain
pitfalls: A sequence that is never consumed does nothing, and every new collection re-executes all stages - expensive or side-effecting stages repeat per iteration.
Stateful operators such as sorted or groupBy buffer the whole sequence and erase the memory advantage of lazy processing.
Sequences are single-pass in practice and hold iterator state; storing one and iterating it twice sees inconsistent behaviour.

variants.name: kotlinx.coroutines Flow pipeline
variants.implementation_notes: A flow is the asynchronous version of the same shape: an emitter produces values, intermediate operators consume upstream values and return a new downstream flow, and a collector consumes the result; intermediate operators are cold and set up the chain, terminal operators such as collect or toList run it (kotlinlang.org flow docs). Buffer/flowOn introduce concurrency between stages and back it with a channel, so this is the variant for suspend functions and long-lived streams; keep Sequence for synchronous data.
pitfalls: Flows are cold: every collector re-executes the whole pipeline, so shared or expensive streams need shareIn/stateIn.
buffer() and flowOn() change concurrency and ordering; a stage that assumed sequential execution can now interleave.
Exceptions cancel the whole flow; catch() only sees upstream failures, so a failing downstream collector cannot be rescued inside the chain.
